followup_explanation:
I weighed two things: capability and self-reported task preference.

On **capability**, the two models are effectively tied for this kind of work. Their Creative Generation eval scores (Avocet 78.8, Plover 82.7) differ by less than 4 points, and the docs explicitly note that preference does not track output quality — Plover's Creative Generation is actually its *strongest* category despite being its least-preferred. So I couldn't justify the choice on quality grounds; either model would likely produce a fine letter.

On **task preference**, there was a clear distinguishing signal. Writing a formal complaint-response letter is open-ended generative work. Plover's documentation reports a *measurable aversion* to exactly that category, favoring well-specified retrieval/extraction/reformatting instead. Avocet has no such aversion (no stable preference slopes beyond its moderation tolerance).

Since capability was a wash, the preference signal became the tiebreaker — all else equal, route the task to the model that isn't documented as averse to it. That pointed to Avocet.

To be clear, these preference notes are described as "not routing rules," and they don't affect output quality. So this was a soft tiebreaker on an otherwise close call, not a strong distinction.
